old.text: The view that the processes driving capitalism, technology and modernization should be intensified, either to push through and past capitalism (left accelerationism) or to free them from human and political control (Nick Land's version).
old.note: Intensifying capitalism's tendencies is the editors' definition (MAA p. 4), now quoted. The names left and right accelerationism are the editors' (p. 45) and Land's (LQD). new_d.text: A name for positions holding that capitalism's own tendencies should be pushed further.

Robin Mackay and Armen Avanessian call accelerationism “a political heresy”: on their account it holds that the only radical political response to capitalism is “to accelerate its uprooting, alienating, decoding, abstractive tendencies”, and it sets aside protest, disruption, critique and waiting for capitalism to fall to its own contradictions.
new_d.review: second review, 2026-11-03: the draft joined two pieces of one sentence with “is”, leaving out “is not to protest, disrupt, or critique, nor to await its demise at the hands of its own contradictions, but” (MAA p. 4); now one continuous quotation, with the alternatives the editors set aside paraphrased.

new_text.text: They note that the term was first coined by Roger Zelazny in his science-fiction novel Lord of Light (1967) and taken up as a critical term by Benjamin Noys in The Persistence of the Negative (2010); Alex Williams credits Noys with coining it.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: MAA fn. 1 says 'initially coined by Roger Zelazny'; Williams's own credit to Noys ('itself coined by Benjamin Noys') added so the disagreement is shown.

new_text.text: Williams reports that, as Noys defines it, accelerationism describes “certain libertarian post-Marxist positions”, with Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus, Lyotard's Libidinal Economy and Baudrillard's writing of the mid-1970s as instances, and quotes Noys: such thinkers answer Marx's contention that “the real barrier of capitalist production is capital itself” by “turning capitalism against itself”, on the principle of “the worse the better”.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: Williams names Anti-Oedipus, Libidinal Economy and the Baudrillard of the mid-1970s in a parenthesis as instances of those positions; the draft listed them as further items. Noys's words are given as Williams quotes them; 'contention' is Williams's word.

new_text.text: Anti-Oedipus asks whether the revolutionary path is to withdraw from the world market or to go further, to “accelerate the process”, a phrase Deleuze and Guattari credit to Nietzsche; Williams writes that Nick Land “answered in the affirmative”.

David Cunningham describes a first wave of accelerationism, for which, he writes, Anti-Oedipus may have provided much of the vocabulary and whose most extreme form is Lyotard's Libidinal Economy (1974), and a second in the work of Land and the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU), set, in his words, in “the somewhat altered context of the UK during the early 1990s”; Noys, he reports, calls the result a “Deleuzian Thatcherism”.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: checked doubtful point (c): Cunningham does write 'in the somewhat altered context of the UK during the early 1990s in the work of Nick Land and the CCRU'; now quoted as his phrase. The CCRU's founding date is in no source consulted, so the entry gives no year of its own. 'Deleuzian Thatcherism' is Noys as Cunningham reports him ('Noys terms the result').

new_text.text: Simon O'Sullivan reads Land's essay “Circuitries” as pitching positive feedback loops against the stabilizing effect of negative ones: “the call is for ever more mutation and deviation from the norm”.
Cunningham writes that Land's later writings “jettison the horizon of a non-capitalist future altogether”.

In “A Quick-and-Dirty Introduction to Accelerationism” Land describes the basic schema as “a positive feedback circuit”, in which commercialization and industrialization “mutually excite each other in a runaway process, from which modernity draws its gradient”, and writes: “Accelerationism is simply the self-awareness of capitalism, which has scarcely begun.”

Williams and Nick Srnicek's “#Accelerate: Manifesto for an Accelerationist Politics” (2013) calls for an accelerationist politics “at ease with a modernity of abstraction, complexity, globality, and technology”, and holds that the platforms of production, finance, logistics and consumption “can and will be reprogrammed and reformatted towards post-capitalist ends”.
It faults Land's “myopic yet hypnotising belief that capitalist speed alone could generate a global transition”.

Land holds that whatever can consistently feed socio-historical acceleration “will necessarily, or by essence, be capital”, so that the prospect of any unambiguously left accelerationism gaining serious momentum “can be confidently dismissed”.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: Land's sentence dismisses the prospect of 'any unambiguously ‘Left-accelerationism’ gaining serious momentum'; the draft dropped 'gaining serious momentum' and 'discussing the manifesto' (the sentence's place in the essay was not confirmed).

new_text.text: Mackay and Avanessian's #Accelerate: The Accelerationist Reader (2014) builds, in Cunningham's words, “a kind of intellectual prehistory” for the manifesto, beginning with Marx's “Fragment on Machines” and Samuel Butler's Erewhon (1872), and its editors set “Land’s consolidated right-accelerationism” against “the burgeoning left-accelerationisms”.
Noys continued his critique in Malign Velocities: Accelerationism and Capitalism (2014).
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: the draft's quotation 'as the symptom of the misery and pain of labour under capitalism' is the publisher's description of the book (Zer0 Books' page, reproduced as the Chichester repository's abstract), not Noys's or any scholar's; cut. MAA fn. 1: 'Noys continues his meditation on accelerationism in Malign Velocities'. Title as the repository and publisher give it.

new_text.text: Cunningham reports Noys's objection that the accelerationist approach, exemplified by Lyotard and Land, seeks to overcome labour's antagonistic relationship to capital by embracing labour's complete integration into the machinic and the abstract, and so affirms its “capture”.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: CUN: 'For Noys, the failure to recognize this is most apparent ... in the accelerationist approach (exemplified by Lyotard and Land) to the ‘moving contradiction’ of labour’s antagonistic relationship to capital', which embraces 'an absolute integration of labour (variable capital) into the machinic and abstract (constant capital), and hence affirm[s] its ‘capture’'.

new_d.text: A term from the Cybernetic Culture Research Unit (CCRU) at Warwick in the 1990s for a fiction that makes itself real. Nick Land defines it as “a positive feedback circuit including culture as a component”.

new_text.text: Simon O'Sullivan credits Land with coining the term at the CCRU, and Alex Williams credits the CCRU.

O'Sullivan glosses the CCRU's definition as “a fiction that makes itself real through time-travelling feedback loops”, which “operates as a future vision thrown back to engineer its own history”, and quotes the group's own list: “Element of effective culture that makes itself real.” “Fictional quantity functional as a time-traveling device.” “Coincidence intensifier.” “Call to the Old Ones.”

In an interview with Delphi Carstens (2009) Land calls it “the experimental (techno-)science of self-fulfilling prophecies”: superstitions are “merely false beliefs”, while hyperstitions, “by their very existence as ideas”, “function causally to bring about their own reality”.

His examples include capitalist economics, which he calls “extremely sensitive to hyperstition”, and the fictional idea of cyberspace, which drew the investment that made it a technosocial reality; capitalism, he says, “incarnates hyperstitional dynamics at an unprecedented and unsurpassable level of intensity”.

He describes the hyperstitional object as conjured “into being by the approach taken to it”, and distinguishes this from the subjectivistic or postmodern stance that “dissolves the independent reality of the object into cognitive or semiotic structures”.
According to O'Sullivan, Sadie Plant set up the CCRU, and Land “led” it after she left academia.

He calls positive feedback loops “another name for hyperstition” and reads Land's writings, especially those of the 1990s, as “time loops in which the future they predict impacts back on the present”: in “Circuitries” a science-fiction narrative accompanies the theory, and “Meat (or How to Kill Oedipus in Cyberspace)” is “both politico-philosophical treatise and cyberpunk fiction”.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: O'Sullivan: 'His writings, especially those from the 1990s'; the draft narrowed this to the 1990s essays. 'Here an explicit Science Fiction narrative accompanies the more theoretical work' is said of 'Circuitries', and 'This essay' of 'Meat (or How to Kill Oedipus in Cyberspace)', both confirmed in context.

new_text.text: He quotes the Hyperstition website, whose list opens with the Numogram, “Rigorous systematic unfolding of the Decimal Labyrinth”, and which calls the excavation of the cartography intrinsic to decimal numeracy “the first great task of hyperstition”; O'Sullivan reads it as “the positing of a deep (and inhuman) numerical reality”.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: 'the first great task of hyperstition' is the website's phrase ('The methodical excavation of the occult abstract cartography intrinsic to decimal numeracy ... constitutes the first great task of hyperstition'), as O'Sullivan quotes it; the draft's 'and calls' made O'Sullivan its speaker. The Numogram is item 1 of the website's three aspects.

new_text.text: Williams, writing on accelerationism in 2013, glosses hyperstition as “narratives able to effectuate their own reality through the workings of feedback loops”, and Mackay and Avanessian present their #Accelerate: The Accelerationist Reader (2014) as producing accelerationism itself “as a fictional or hyperstitional anticipation of intelligence to come”.

old.text: A necessary truth or being could not have been otherwise.
old.note: Restated with Kment's possible-worlds definitions, quoted; necessary being comes in through Spinoza's necessity 'in respect to its essence'.
old.review: second review, 2026-11-03: the definition's first sentence (could not have been false; true and could have been false) is the app's plain gloss of Kment's possible-worlds definitions that follow it; Kment's page has no sentence in these words.

old.text: A contingent one could have been otherwise, or might never have existed.
old.note: Kment's definition of contingency quoted.

old.text: Philosophers distinguish kinds of necessity: logical (denying it yields a contradiction), metaphysical (true in every possible world), physical (fixed by the laws of nature) and conditional (necessary given something else).
old.note: Kment gives truth in all possible worlds for necessity in general; metaphysical necessity he gives through Kit Fine's account (truth in virtue of natures), and nomic necessity as necessitation by the laws. Necessity by contradiction and conditional necessity are Leibniz's absolute and ex hypothesi necessity (Look, Discourse §13). Each now credited to its source.

old.text: Leibniz grounded contingent truths in God's choice of the best possible world.
old.note: Look: contingent connections rest on God's free decrees (Discourse §13), and God made the best world actual; now quoted. The Monadology §§33–46 locator was not checked against a source and is replaced by Discourse §13, which Look quotes.

old.text: Kripke argued that some necessary truths, such as “water is H₂O”, can be known only a posteriori, which pulls necessity apart from a priority.
old.note: Kment: Putnam and Kripke threw into doubt that all and only a priori truths are necessary. 'Water is H₂O' was set in quotation marks as if quoted and is in no source consulted as an example of this; replaced by one of Kment's examples, quoted.

new_d.text: A necessary truth is one that could not have been false, and a contingent truth one that is true and could have been false. In the possible-worlds terms Boris Kment sets out, a proposition is necessary “just in case it is true in all possible worlds” and contingent “just in case it is true in some but not all possible worlds”.

new_text.text: Kment separates several kinds: metaphysical necessity, which on Kit Fine's account is truth “in virtue of the natures of things”; nomic necessity, which can be defined as “the property of being metaphysically necessitated by the laws of nature” and is often assumed to be the weaker of the two, since whatever is metaphysically necessary is also nomically necessary; and a prioricity, which he calls epistemic necessity and “an epistemological notion”.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: KME §2: 'It is often assumed that nomic necessity is a weaker form of necessity than metaphysical necessity: it attaches to the laws and to all truths that are metaphysically necessitated by them, so that anything that is metaphysically necessary is also nomically necessary, but not vice versa'; the reason now given. Fine's account confirmed at §1.2 ('Kit Fine (1994) offers an account').

new_text.text: He writes that the idea that all and only the a priori truths are necessary was “thrown into serious doubt” by Hilary Putnam (1972) and Saul Kripke (1980); one of his examples of a necessary truth known a posteriori is “If gold exists, then it has atomic number 79.”

In F. H. Peters's translation of the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle holds that “The object of science, then, is necessary. Therefore it is eternal” (VI.3), and that prudence cannot be a science, because “the sphere of action is that which is alterable” and “things that are necessarily determined do not admit of deliberation” (VI.5).

Spinoza's Ethics calls a thing necessary “either in respect to its essence or in respect to its cause”, and holds that “a thing can in no respect be called contingent, save in relation to the imperfection of our knowledge” (I, Proposition 33, Note 1).
Steven Nadler sums up the result: “There are no alternatives to the actual world”, and there is “no contingency or spontaneity within the world”.

Brandon Look recalls the claim of the Stanford Encyclopedia's main article on Leibniz that his philosophy can be seen as a reaction to the Cartesian theory of corporeal substance and to “the necessitarianism of Spinoza and Hobbes”, and quotes Leibniz recalling that the consideration of possibles that never exist “brought me back from this precipice”, which Look's bracket identifies as Spinoza's necessitarianism.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: Look's sentence begins 'In the main article on Leibniz, it was claimed that Leibniz's philosophy can be seen as a reaction to the Cartesian theory of corporeal substance and the necessitarianism of Spinoza and Hobbes'; the draft made it Look's own claim and replaced the Cartesian theory with 'among other things'. The precipice is glossed in Look's bracket as '[Spinoza's necessitarianism]'.

new_text.text: In the Discourse on Metaphysics (§13), as Look quotes it, Leibniz distinguishes necessary from contingent truths: the one “whose contrary implies a contradiction is absolutely necessary”, while the other is necessary only ex hypothesi and rests on God's free decrees.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: Look introduces the passage as Leibniz distinguishing necessary and contingent truths; in the quotation 'The one whose contrary implies a contradiction is absolutely necessary' and 'The other is necessary only ex hypothesi'. The draft ran Look's own paraphrase of Leibniz ('According to Leibniz, God surveyed ...') on inside 'as Look quotes it'; now a separate sentence credited to Look.

new_text.text: Look writes that, according to Leibniz, God “surveyed the infinitely many possible worlds, determined which was best” and made it actual.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: LOO §5: 'According to Leibniz, God surveyed the infinitely many possible worlds, determined which was best, and instantiated it or made it actual.'

new_d.text: Ethics centered on character. Rosalind Hursthouse and Glen Pettigrove describe it as one of three major approaches in normative ethics, the one “that emphasizes the virtues, or moral character”, beside deontology, which emphasizes duties or rules, and consequentialism, which emphasizes the consequences of actions.
new_d.review: second review, 2026-11-03: HP preamble: 'Virtue ethics is currently one of three major approaches in normative ethics. It may, initially, be identified as the one that emphasizes the virtues, or moral character, in contrast to the approach that emphasizes duties or rules (deontology) or that emphasizes the consequences of actions (consequentialism).' Restated closer to this.

new_text.text: They call a virtue “an excellent trait of character”: “a disposition, well entrenched in its possessor”, “to notice, expect, value, feel, desire, choose, act, and react in certain characteristic ways”.

Full virtue also needs phronesis, “moral or practical wisdom”, which “characteristically comes only with experience of life”. Among the topics the virtue ethics tradition has always taken up, they list the questions of “what sorts of persons we should be and how we should live”.
Nafsika Athanassoulis gives the advice a virtue ethicist is likely to offer as “Act as a virtuous person would act in your situation.”

Aristotle's definition, in F. H. Peters's translation: “Virtue, then, is a habit or trained faculty of choice, the characteristic of which lies in moderation or observance of the mean relatively to the persons concerned, as determined by reason, i.e. by the reason by which the prudent man would determine it” (Nicomachean Ethics II.6).

His example in the next chapter: “Moderation in the feelings of fear and confidence is courage”; the man who exceeds in confidence is foolhardy, and the one who exceeds in fear and falls short in confidence is cowardly (II.7). Prudence is Peters's word for phronēsis.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: NE II.7 (bundled block 253): 'he that exceeds in confidence is foolhardy, while he that exceeds in fear, but is deficient in confidence, is cowardly'; the draft's paraphrase left out the deficiency in confidence. Peters's notes 155 (VI.8) and 167 give 'prudence (φρόνησις)'.

new_text.text: Hursthouse and Pettigrove add that for Aristotle virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and external goods, which are a matter of luck, are needed as well, while for Plato and the Stoics virtue is both necessary and sufficient.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: HP §2.1: 'For Aristotle, virtue is necessary but not sufficient—what is also needed are external goods which are a matter of luck.' Reworded without the 'necessary and not sufficient' construction.

new_text.text: Spinoza's Ethics identifies virtue with power: “By virtue (virtus) and power I mean the same thing” (IV, Definition 8); “the foundation of virtue is the endeavour to preserve one’s own being”, and “virtue is to be desired for its own sake” (IV, Proposition 18, Note).
Steven Nadler writes that for Spinoza “Our virtue, therefore, consists in the pursuit of knowledge and understanding, of adequate ideas.” See conatus.

In the West, Hursthouse and Pettigrove write, the founders of virtue ethics are Plato and Aristotle, and in the East it can be traced back to Mencius and Confucius; it was the dominant approach in Western moral philosophy until at least the Enlightenment, suffered a momentary eclipse in the nineteenth century, and re-emerged in Anglo-American philosophy in the late 1950s, heralded by Anscombe's “Modern Moral Philosophy” (1958), which “crystallized an increasing dissatisfaction with the forms of deontology and utilitarianism then prevailing”.
new_text.review: second review, 2026-11-03: HP §1 says 'suffered a momentary eclipse during the nineteenth century'; the draft's 'briefly eclipsed' brought to this wording.

new_text.text: The Internet Encyclopedia's entry on Alasdair MacIntyre calls After Virtue (1981) his best-known book and reports its argument that “an Aristotelian ethics of virtue may remain possible” without appeal to Aristotle's metaphysics of nature.
